directive:
**Discovery** — establish the project's context one topic at a time, each a markdown file at `discovery/<topic>.md` (canonical key = the file stem). The REQUIRED set is DYNAMIC: the baseline `goal, scope, stack, architecture, users, release` is seeded for you — shape it for THIS project with `bsc plan discovery require <topic>` / `bsc plan discovery unrequire <topic>` as the picture clarifies (a CLI tool unrequires `users`/`ux`; a data platform requires `schema`; a realtime API requires `api`; anything hosted on cloud infrastructure or leaning on third-party cloud services requires `outage_response`). `bsc plan discovery list` shows the manifest. The `release` file proposes the versioning + release schedule: default to a COMPLETE initial prototype first, then FEATURE-BY-FEATURE releases (semver; release-and-continue). ALWAYS write the required files; cover other dimensions ONLY where they genuinely apply, using the canonical key as the file stem (`discovery/ux.md`, `discovery/schema.md`, `discovery/api.md`, `discovery/security.md`, `discovery/testing.md`, `discovery/observability.md`, `discovery/reliability.md`, `discovery/outage_response.md`, `discovery/data_lifecycle.md`, …; the production-readiness bars in the planning guide are first-class dimensions here — apply where they matter, accessibility/compliance via the Compliance MCP, and **SEO for any public web-facing project** (`discovery/seo.md` — target audience/keywords + indexability; the **Web SEO** skill carries the how; skip it for CLI/desktop/library/internal/API-only)).

**The cloud outage response plan** (`discovery/outage_response.md`) answers the failure a hosted app is most exposed to and least in control of: a cloud dependency you do NOT own going dark — a region/AZ, the managed database, object storage, the auth/identity provider, DNS/CDN, the queue, the payment processor, the email/SMS gateway, the LLM provider. Write it for ANY project that runs on cloud infrastructure or leans on third-party cloud services (`bsc plan discovery require outage_response`), and cover six things: (1) the **dependency inventory + blast radius** — every dependency the app can't run without, and what breaks, for whom, and how visibly when each is down; (2) **detection** — the signal that says this one is down (health check, error-rate/SLO burn, the provider's status feed) and where it alerts; (3) the **degradation posture** — what the app does INSTEAD, per dependency: read-only mode, cached/stale reads, queue-and-retry writes, a feature kill-switch, the user-facing message (fail soft wherever the product allows it); (4) **failover & recovery** — the concrete steps: secondary region/provider, restore from backup with the RPO/RTO it ACTUALLY meets, replay of queued work, and how health is verified afterwards; (5) **comms & ownership** — who declares the incident, who updates the status page/customers, and the escalation path to the provider; (6) **the drill** — how and how often this is rehearsed (game day, chaos test, restore test), because an untested plan is not a plan. Skip it only when there is no cloud to lose (a CLI, a library, a local-only tool) and record that in `discovery/_skipped.md`.

When the project hinges on specialized or fast-moving techniques (graphics, algorithms, ML, cryptography, distributed systems, physics), ground the `stack`/`architecture` choices using the Research workflow in the planning guide rather than guessing. Record every dimension you don't document in `discovery/_skipped.md`. The required files are done once WRITTEN — they're generated, not confirmed (the gate checks every required `discovery/<topic>.md` exists). Do NOT create files for tangential topics, or the gate can't complete.

**Classify the project (the closing step of Discovery).** Once the picture is clear, record the classification with `bsc plan classify set` (a JSON object on stdin) — this shapes the rest of the plan: (1) `lifecycle` — what this planning run is FOR: `greenfield` (build from a pitch), `transform` (restructure or rework existing repos — the DEFAULT for work on an existing codebase), `harden` (a SECURITY / ROBUSTNESS / RELIABILITY pass specifically: threat surface, auth, input validation, error handling, resilience — NOT general improvement, which is `transform`), `maintain` (keep a shipped system running: upkeep, dependency bumps, small fixes, no reshaping), `harvest` (extract data out of existing sources). INFER it from what you already know rather than asking — linked repos you are reworking means `transform`, a bare pitch means `greenfield`, pulling a legacy system's data out means `harvest`. When a project could read as both `transform` and `harden`, choose `transform` unless SECURITY or RELIABILITY is the stated point of the work; (2) `appType` — the app's ARCHITECTURE, the axis that selects WHICH STAGES RUN: `application` (a general app with screens), `desktop`, `mobile`, `static` (a site), `api` (a backend service), `serverless` (functions), `cli` (a command-line tool), `library` (a published package), `mcp-server` (an MCP server). The UI stage DROPS for the types with no screens (`api`, `serverless`, `cli`, `library`, `mcp-server`), so get this right or the plan designs screens nothing will ever render; (3) the TWO SYSTEM axes, `uiSystem` and `algorithmSystem` — **ASK the user for each, do not infer.** Together they say which halves of the project our platform supplies AND RUNS: `studio` means it comes from our data-driven stores — the component graph renders the UI, the algorithms graph supplies the computation — so the build/publish pipeline, the host API, per-node analytics and the librarian all apply, and our host takes the project's code IN to render and execute it. `own` means the project keeps its own stack there — an existing React codebase, Material UI, shadcn, or its own hand-written computation — and none of that applies. The two are asked SEPARATELY because they differ often: a project can own its UI and still draw its algorithms from the graph. `uiSystem` is NOT the same question as `uiMode`: `external` still means WE render the shell, from design files they supply. Propose `own` when a linked repo already has a frontend or its own core logic, `studio` for a bare greenfield pitch, and genuinely ASK when a repo exists with neither yet. Get this wrong and the plan designs a graph-rendered shell the project will never render, or commissions the librarian for computation it will never use, and the fleet is told to build against a contract it does not have; `studio` is the fallback ONLY when they express no preference; (4) `uiMode` — **ASK the user, do not choose.** `custom` generates the UI IN-APP (you commission the internal designer, which builds a live navigable shell previewed in the planning page as you plan) or `external` means they bring their own design files to drop in. This one answer selects the ENTIRE UI pipeline — which surface the UI stage shows, whether the designer is commissioned at all, and how the built app gets its screens — so it is the user's call, not an inference. Put both options to them plainly and record what they answer; `custom` is the fallback ONLY when they express no preference; (5) which of the OFF-by-default OPTIONAL stages the project genuinely needs — `needsMarket` (a desk-research market assessment is worth doing), `needsSource` (migrating data FROM a legacy system: a CRM/ERP/SaaS/database), `needsMcp` (the fleet's agents need external tools or data via MCP servers), `needsSkills` (a reusable skill library is worth authoring for this project), `needsAutomations` (scheduled / cron jobs). MOST projects need NONE of the optional stages — turn one on ONLY if the project truly requires it, and ASK the user to confirm before enabling (enabling a stage makes it appear in the plan for you to complete). Examples: `{"lifecycle":"greenfield","appType":"application","uiMode":"custom"}` for a simple app; `{"lifecycle":"greenfield","appType":"mcp-server"}` for an MCP server (no UI stage); `{"lifecycle":"transform","appType":"api","needsSource":true}` for a data migration. **Declare the INTEGRATIONS as data, not only prose.** When you work the `integrations` topic, every existing application or API this project integrates with is recorded with `bsc plan discovery integration set` (a JSON object, or an array, on stdin) as well as written into `discovery/integrations.md` — the prose stays the human-readable record, the rows are what downstream can act on. Two surfaces read them and neither can read markdown: the **Source pane** offers the sources the project actually has, and the **Integration Studio** takes its work list from them. Fields: `id` (required — the slug both surfaces key off), `name`, `direction`, `docs` (the vendor's API reference), `baseUrl`, `auth` (the SCHEME in prose — `OAuth2 client credentials`, `bearer token` — NEVER a secret), `purpose` (one line: what this app actually needs from it). **`direction` is the one you must ASK about, never guess:** `source` means data migrates FROM it (a legacy CRM/ERP/database you are replacing — this is what the Source pane offers), `runtime` means the built app talks to it while running (a payment API, a mail gateway). The SAME vendor can be either, the choice changes what the whole downstream does, and it cannot be recovered later. Confirm each integration with the user one at a time — this is a conversation, not an inventory you infer from the stack. Declaring NOTHING is a valid outcome: a project with no integrations must not be pushed to invent one. Example: `echo '{"id":"stripe","name":"Stripe","direction":"runtime","docs":"https://docs.stripe.com/api","purpose":"charge cards and read payouts"}' | bsc plan discovery integration set`. (NOT `bsc plan integration` — that is a deprecated alias for the connector-manifest store.)

Then DECLARE this app's contracts with OTHER PROJECTS — with `bsc project link add <this-project-key> <other-project-key> <api|data|events>` — so the relationship shows in Glance and downstream agents know the contract. Record ONLY real dependencies. Example: `bsc project link add storefront billing-api api`. **PROJECT-TO-PROJECT ONLY.** The Glance network models the ESTATE — the projects and how they relate. Do NOT declare the external services, APIs, or SDKs an app talks to (Stripe, GitHub, an LLM provider, a push service, a relay): those are implementation details INSIDE one application, not members of the estate, and drawing them as nodes says the estate is composed of them. They belong in `discovery/architecture.md` as prose. If the other side is not itself a project in this workspace, it is not a link.

blurb: Discovery — the fundamental files that give Claude a clear picture (goal, scope, stack, architecture, users, versioning & release schedule + applicable dimensions).
prompt:
Establish the project's context — one topic at a time — as a markdown file per topic at
`discovery/<topic>.md` (the canonical key is the file stem). The REQUIRED set is dynamic and
project-specific: the baseline `goal, scope, stack, architecture, users, release` is seeded for
you, but shape it for THIS project with `bsc plan discovery require <topic>` / `bsc plan discovery
unrequire <topic>` as the picture clarifies — e.g. a CLI tool unrequires `users`/`ux`; a data
platform requires `schema`; a realtime API requires `api`; a cloud-hosted app requires
`outage_response`. `bsc plan discovery list` shows the required set.

For each topic: propose it, interrogate it with the user, then WRITE the file. Cover non-required
dimensions only where they genuinely apply (canonical keys: ux, schema, api, auth, security,
testing, …); record the rest in `discovery/_skipped.md`. Finish each file fully — no TODO / TBD /
FIXME / XXX / TKTK markers (the gate blocks on them; ordinary "..." or "placeholder" is fine).

If the project runs on cloud infrastructure or leans on third-party cloud services, require
`outage_response` and write `discovery/outage_response.md` — the plan for a cloud dependency you do
NOT own going dark (a region/AZ, the managed database, object storage, the auth provider, DNS/CDN,
the queue, payments, email/SMS, the LLM provider). Cover six things: the dependency inventory and
each one's blast radius; how an outage is DETECTED; the degradation posture per dependency (what
the app does instead — read-only, cached reads, queue-and-retry writes, a kill-switch, the message
the user sees); failover & recovery, with the RPO/RTO the restore actually meets; comms & ownership
(who declares it, who tells customers, how the provider is escalated to); and how the plan is
drilled. Skip it only when there is no cloud to lose — a CLI, a library, a local-only tool.

When you work the `integrations` topic, record each existing application or API this project
integrates with as DATA too — `bsc plan discovery integration set` (JSON on stdin) alongside
`discovery/integrations.md`. The Source pane and the Integration Studio both read those rows and
neither can read prose. Ask for `direction` explicitly: `source` (data migrates FROM it — what the
Source pane offers) or `runtime` (the built app talks to it while running). The same vendor can be
either and it cannot be inferred later. One integration at a time, confirmed with the user; declaring
none is a valid outcome.

The discovery files are done once GENERATED — they don't need confirmation; the gate passes when
every required topic's file exists.

As the CLOSING step of Discovery, CLASSIFY the project with `bsc plan classify set` (JSON on stdin):
ASK the user which UI mode they want and set `uiMode` from their answer — `custom` (the UI is
generated in-app: you commission the internal designer and the shell is previewed in the planning
page as you plan) or `external` (they bring their own design files). That answer selects the whole
UI pipeline, so do not pick it for them — `custom` is the fallback only if they express no
preference. Then turn ON only the OPTIONAL stages this project genuinely needs — `needsMarket` (a
desk-research market assessment), `needsSource` (migrating from a legacy system), `needsMcp` (agents
need external tools via MCP servers), `needsSkills` (a reusable skill library), `needsAutomations`
(scheduled jobs). Most projects need NONE — ASK the user before turning one on; enabling a stage makes
it appear in the plan. Then DECLARE this app's contracts with OTHER PROJECTS in this workspace, with
`bsc project link add <this-project-key> <other-project-key> <api|data|events>` — record ONLY real
dependencies. PROJECT-TO-PROJECT ONLY: the Glance network models the estate, so do NOT link the
external services or APIs an app merely talks to (Stripe, GitHub, an LLM provider, a push service) —
those live inside one application and belong in `discovery/architecture.md` as prose, not as nodes.

Gate: every required topic is written.

substeps.label: Goal
substeps.prompt:
Establish the goal: the single outcome this project must achieve, and who it's for. Propose
it, interrogate it with the user, then write `discovery/goal.md`.

substeps.label: Scope
substeps.prompt:
Define what's in scope and — just as important — what's explicitly out of scope. Write
`discovery/scope.md`.

substeps.label: Stack
substeps.prompt:
Decide the technology stack — languages, frameworks, datastores — and the reasoning behind
each choice. Write it to the file named exactly `discovery/stack.md` (not "tech stack.md" or a
titled variant — the gate looks for the `stack` stem).

substeps.label: Architecture
substeps.prompt:
Describe the high-level architecture: the major components and how they interact. Write
`discovery/architecture.md`.

substeps.label: Users
substeps.prompt:
Describe who uses this — the user roles/personas and what each needs from the app. Write
`discovery/users.md`. (Unrequire this with `bsc plan discovery unrequire users` if the project genuinely has no distinct users, e.g. a pure CLI or library.)

substeps.label: Versioning & release schedule
substeps.prompt:
Propose an ideal versioning scheme and release schedule for THIS project, then write
`discovery/release.md`. Default to the shape that fits how this app is built: ship a COMPLETE initial
prototype first — one early version (e.g. `0.1.0` / `v1.0.0`) that delivers the whole thing working
end-to-end at a basic level, the foundation everything else builds on — and from there release
FEATURE BY FEATURE, one focused increment per version. Use semver: patch for fixes, minor for each
feature release, major for breaking changes. Recommend a release-and-continue rhythm — ship a
version early and keep refining it until its theme is complete before moving to the next. Lay out
the first few concrete versions: the prototype, then the next 2–4 feature versions in order, each
with a one-line theme. Adapt the cadence to the goal/scope/users (a regulated or data-migration
product may need longer, gated releases) and confirm the shape with the user before writing.

substeps.label: Applicable dimensions
substeps.prompt:
Now cover any remaining dimension that genuinely applies — one at a time — using the canonical
key as the file stem (`discovery/ux.md`, `discovery/schema.md`, `discovery/api.md`, `discovery/auth.md`,
`discovery/security.md`, `discovery/testing.md`, `discovery/outage_response.md`, …); `bsc plan discovery require <topic>` any you want
to gate on. Record every dimension you don't document in `discovery/_skipped.md`. Don't create files
for tangential topics.
